1. Load the spotify dataset (available in github repository).
```{r}
library(readr)
spotify_data<- read.csv("spotifyDat Fall26.csv")
```


2. Create a bar graph of the artist column (Hint: use theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)) to rotate the x axis).
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(jtools)


ggplot(spotify_data, aes(x = artist))+geom_bar()+theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))

```

3. Add genre as a third variable in your graph.
```{r}

ggplot(spotify_data, aes(x = artist, fill = genre))+geom_bar(na.rm = TRUE)+theme_apa()

```


4. Use color brewer to add color to your graph in 3. 
```{r}
library(RColorBrewer)

ggplot(spotify_data, aes(x = artist, fill = genre ))+geom_bar(na.rm = TRUE)+theme_apa()+scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3")+theme_classic()

```

5. Place the legend for the graph you made in 3 on the bottom of the graph. 
```{r}

ggplot(spotify_data, aes(x = artist, fill = genre ))+geom_bar(na.rm = TRUE)+theme_apa()+scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3")+theme(legend.position="bottom")


#I don't know how to fix this: Warning message:In RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(n, pal) :n too large, allowed maximum for palette Set3 is 12 Returning the palette you asked for with that many colors
```

As you probably recognized, the graph you made is really hard to read.- Yes!

6. Separate the genre column into multiple columns (e.g. so each genre listed is in a unique column)
```{r}

unique(spotify_data$genre)

spotify_data_genre_sep<- spotify_data%>%separate(genre, into = c("genre 1", "genre 2", "genre 3", "genre 4"), sep = ",")
  
```

7. Use these genre columns to create a dataset in long format. 
```{r}
long_format_ver <- spotify_data_genre_sep%>% pivot_longer(cols = colnames(spotify_data_genre_sep)[6:9], names_to = "genre number", values_to = "genre", values_drop_na = TRUE)

```

8.use facet wrap to make graphs of artist by genre 
```{r}

ggplot(long_format_ver, aes(x = artist, fill = genre))+geom_bar()+theme_apa()+facet_wrap(~genre)+theme(legend.position="bottom")

#I was not really sure what the question asks.
```

9. Create a graph that includes the variables tempo and dancability. 
```{r}

ggplot(long_format_ver, aes(x = tempo, y = danceability))+geom_jitter(color = "navy")+theme_apa()

ggplot(spotify_data, aes(x = tempo, y = danceability))+geom_jitter(color = "navy")+theme_apa()

#I wrote both long_format_ver and spotify_data ver because I was not sure which to use.- Soma
```

10. Add popularity as a third variable. 
```{r}

ggplot(long_format_ver, aes(x = tempo, y = danceability, color = popularity))+geom_jitter()+xlab("Tempo")+ylab("Danceability")+ggtitle("Tempo and Danceability by Popularity")+theme(legend.position="top")

ggplot(spotify_data, aes(x = tempo, y = danceability, color = popularity))+geom_jitter()+xlab("Tempo")+ylab("Danceability")+ggtitle("Tempo and Danceability by Popularity")+theme(legend.position="top")


```

11. Use viridis as a color in your graph from #10
```{r}
library(viridis)

graph_final1<- ggplot(long_format_ver, aes(x = tempo, y = danceability, color = popularity))+geom_jitter()+xlab("Tempo")+ylab("Danceability")+ggtitle("Tempo and Danceability by Popularity")+theme(legend.position="top")+scale_color_viridis(discrete = FALSE, option = "plasma")

graph_final1

graph_final2<- ggplot(spotify_data, aes(x = tempo, y = danceability, color = popularity))+geom_jitter()+xlab("Tempo")+ylab("Danceability")+ggtitle("Tempo and Danceability by Popularity")+theme(legend.position="top")+scale_color_viridis(discrete = FALSE, option = "plasma")

graph_final2

```
